summary: European artists' groups, including IMPALA and Adami, warn that a 2020 CJEU ruling ended the "reciprocity principle" for performance royalties in EU member states. US artists and labels can now collect EU radio and public performance royalties, while Europeans get nothing from US terrestrial radio because the US has no such right. IMPALA estimates an annual loss of about €125m (USD $137m) and up to 40% of income in some countries, and the groups urge the European Commission to propose a fix.
one_line: European artists' groups warn a 2020 CJEU ruling ending royalty reciprocity could shift about $137m a year to US rightsholders unless the EU changes its law.
key_facts: IMPALA estimates the annual loss to EU recorded music rightsholders at approximately €125 million (USD $137m), money that would go to US counterparts.
Artists could lose up to 40% of their income from terrestrial radio and public performances in some countries, matching the share of US music played on the radio there.
In Europe, performance royalties for terrestrial radio and venues are paid to artists and labels as well as songwriters and publishers; in the US they go only to songwriters and publishers.
The reciprocity principle is written into treaties such as the WIPO Performances and Phonograms Treaty of 1996.

In 2020 the CJEU ruled that the reciprocity principle no longer applies to EU member states, because the Rental/Lending Directive of 2006 doesn't allow them to withhold payments to nationals of non-EU countries.
The CJEU said it is for the EU legislature alone to decide on such a limitation, so the EU can change this by rewriting the directive.
The artists' groups issued their statement on Tuesday, November 28, 2023, saying the European Commission has acknowledged concerns and promised a balanced solution but has proposed none.

The Netherlands was the first EU country to stop applying the reciprocity principle, and Will Maas of Ntb/Kunstenbond reports a clear and substantial drop in revenue to Dutch and other European performers and producers.
The US Congress extended copyright to sound recordings in 1971 but without a public performance right.
The Digital Performance Right in Sound Recordings Act of 1995 limited performance rights to digital audio transmissions, which exclude terrestrial radio.
The artists' groups say the US is the only significant music economy in the world without these full rights in its domestic legislation.
IMPALA Executive Chair Helen Smith called for the EU to act and to exert increased trade pressure on the USA to raise its level of copyright protection.
